I have mediated business disputes for twenty years, and almost every difficult conversation is decided in the first ten seconds. Most people start by defending their own position. They explain why they are right, and the other side stops listening immediately, because they are already preparing their answer. So I always start the same way. Before I say anything about the problem, I say, I understand why you are upset. That is not the same as I agree with you. I may not agree at all. But people can only hear a solution after they feel heard. Once they feel heard, I can say, however, and disagree as clearly as I need to. The tension goes down, and the conversation can move from who is right to what we do next.

Last year one of our shipments arrived three weeks late, and a client almost cancelled the whole contract. I was furious with the supplier, and on the first call I started by telling them they were wrong. That was a mistake. They defended themselves, I defended myself, and after an hour we had a list of everything that went wrong and no new date. On the second call, I tried something different. I said, I understand this was not easy for your team either. Then I said, however, we need a date we can trust. We never agreed on whose fault it was, and we decided to agree to disagree on that. But we agreed on a new date in ten minutes, and the client stayed.

First, you listen to each side alone and write down the grievance and the position. Then, you open the call by acknowledging both people before you talk about any solution. After that, you disagree with the ideas that do not work, politely, without taking sides. Next, you agree to disagree on the past, so that the call does not go back to old sore points. Finally, you end with a compromise that both sides can accept, and you put it in writing.
